In the United States, the amount of maternity leave mothers are entitled to depends on their employer, state, and employment status. At the federal level, the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) provides up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave for eligible employees who work for companies with at least 50 employees [d5][d6][d7]. However, this protection does not cover all workers — approximately 40% of women do not qualify for FMLA, meaning only about half of all working women in the U.S. receive job protection under this statute [d3][d5]. Federal government employees receive a more generous benefit: up to 12 weeks of paid parental leave under the Federal Employee Paid Leave Act (FEPLA), which took effect on October 1, 2020 [d2][d7]. Beyond federal law, entitlements vary significantly by state and employer — several states including California, New York, New Jersey, Massachusetts, Washington, and others guarantee some form of paid family leave, and some states like California add up to 4 months of pregnancy disability leave on top of parental leave [d6][d7]. Notably, the U.S. is the only high-income country that does not mandate paid maternity leave nationally [d8], and the current U.S. average of about 70 days falls far short of UNICEF's recommended 168 days (24 weeks) and the International Labor Organization's minimum recommendation of 18 weeks [d4].
